facts.raw_span: 2 progressively enlarging, painless nodular lesions on the forehead and right cheek
initially observed as erythematous nodules 3 months prior
lesions gradually increased in size with subsequent central ulceration and blackish crusting
No fever, pain, or discharge from the lesions was noted
history of kidney transplant in 2004 causing immunocompromised status
Two distinct lesions measuring 2 × 2 cm each were identified over the glabella and right cheek
lesions were firm with central ulceration with hemorrhagic crusting
Dermoscopy showed arborizing telangiectasias, central ulceration with crusting, and peripheral pigment
Extensive dermal collection of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and macrophages
Intracellular yeasts with surrounding halos were identified
Computed tomography of chest and abdomen showed no involvement of internal organs
Polymerase chain reaction analysis of tissue specimen was performed

concepts.why: The presence of intracellular yeasts with surrounding halos, as seen in the histopathological examination, is characteristic of Cryptococcosis, particularly in an immunocompromised patient.

The combination of skin lesions with central ulceration, hemorrhagic crusting, and dermoscopic findings of arborizing telangiectasias, along with the histopathological evidence of intracellular yeasts, supports the diagnosis of Cutaneous Cryptococcosis.

Although the computed tomography of chest and abdomen showed no involvement of internal organs, the patient's immunocompromised status and the presence of multiple skin lesions suggest the possibility of Disseminated Cryptococcosis, which may not have yet involved internal organs.

The clinical presentation of skin lesions with central ulceration and hemorrhagic crusting, along with the histopathological findings, is consistent with Cryptococcal cellulitis, a localized skin infection caused by Cryptococcus species.
The patient's immunocompromised status due to kidney transplant increases the risk of opportunistic skin infections, including those caused by fungi such as Cryptococcus species.
